doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: Learning to improvise in church
summary: The church role of the single instrument, ear training, and sneaking Coltrane and Rollins ideas into church playing.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Let me just go back for a second to the connection between the church music and what you aspired to. It’s interesting, what you were playing in the church had to be somewhat improvised, as far as your role.

Of course. Me being like a single instrument, my role was to improvise, and to make it hot, and to phrase melodies when people — sometime when church people, they’ll start off a song, and my mother was very good at this, they’d start a song off in about three different keys. They said [sings] I’m a soldier in the Army of the Lord. And somewhere in there you’ve got to decide which kind of key you’re going to play in. And my mother

was very good at that, and to just nail it from the onset. She’d get the best of — the strongest tone they sang, she would make that the center. And I got good at it too after a while. And there was a lot of ear training going on there, because people, they come to church to sing and 99% of them can’t sing at all, but they have a lot of enthusiasm.
But the idea that you’re playing improvised music but you can’t play jazz. Your mother didn’t like that. What was the distinction?

Well as long as I was playing the church music and improvising it wasn’t considered jazz. Like I mean I was getting into John Coltrane and Sonny Rollins and all these people, and I was putting that into the church. They didn’t know I was really getting into that. All they knew was that as long as I could play the church melodies fine, whatever else I played, they didn’t care. They didn’t even know if it was jazz or not. They didn’t care. But they knew that it was good. But they knew that when it came to playing that melody that I could play it strong. That was the point. So I got away with that I guess you could say. But that’s where I learned to improvise, in the church. It’s true.
